notes.text: To see Saul — That is, to visit him, in token of respect or friendship: or, to seek counsel from God for him. Otherwise he did see him chap. xix, 24. Though indeed it was not Samuel that came thither with design to see Saul, but Saul went thither to see Samuel, and that accidentally. Samuel is appointed to anoint one of the sons of Jesse king, ver. 1-5. The elder sons are passed by, and David anointed, ver. 6- 13. Saul growing melancholy is eased by David's music, ver. 14- 23.

Mourn — And pray for his restitution, which the following words imply he did. Oil - Which was used in the inauguration of kings. But here it is used in the designation of a king; for David was not actually made king by it, but still remained a subject. And the reason of this anticipation was the comfort of Samuel, and other good men, against their fears in case of Saul's death, and the assurance of David's title, which otherwise would have been doubtful. I have provided - This phrase is very emphatical, and implies the difference between this and the former king. Saul was a king of the people's providing, he was the product of their sinful desires: but this is a king of my own providing, to fulfil all my will, and to serve my glory.

Trembled — Because it was strange and unexpected to them, this being but an obscure town, and remote from Samuel, and therefore they justly thought there was some extraordinary reason for it. Peaceable - The Hebrew phrase, comest thou in peace, is as much as to say (in our phrase) is all well?

He sanctified — It seems evident that there was something peculiar in Jesse's invitation. For first, both he and his sons were invited, whereas the others were only invited for their own persons. Secondly, the different phrase here used, that he sanctified these, when he only bade the other sanctify themselves; argues a singular care of Samuel in their sanctification. Which makes it probable, that the rest were only to join with them in the act of sacrificing; but these, and only these, were invited to feast upon the remainders of the sacrifices.

Before him — That is, in this place where God is now present. For it is observable, that not only the sacrifice is said to be offered, but even the feast upon the remainders of it is said, to be eaten before the Lord, Deut. xii, 7, that is, before or near his altar, where God was present in a special manner. This I take to be the person I am sent to anoint: wherein yet be was mistaken, as other prophets sometimes were, when they hastily spake their own thoughts, before they had consulted God.
Seven — There are but seven named, 1 Chron. ii, 13-15, because one of them was either born of a concubine: or, died immediately after this time.

Keepeth sheep — And consequently is the most unfit of all my sons for that high employment. Either therefore he did not understand David's wisdom and valour, or he judged him unfit, by reason of his mean education. And God so ordered it by his providence, that David's choice might plainly appear to be God's work, and not Samuel's, or Jesse's. David signifies beloved: a fit name for so eminent a type of the Beloved Son. It is supposed, David was now about twenty years old. If so, his troubles by Saul lasted near ten years: for he was thirty years old when Saul died. Samuel having done this went to Ramah. He retired to die in peace, since his eyes had seen the salvation, even the scepter brought into the tribe of Judah.

Anointed him — David's brethren saw David's unction, yet did not understand, that he was anointed to the kingdom; but were only told by Samuel, that he was anointed to some great service, which hereafter they should know. Thus Jesse only, and David, understood the whole business, and his brethren were able to attest to that act of Samuel's anointing him, which, with other collateral evidences, was abundantly sufficient to prove David's right to the kingdom, if need should be. The spirit,&c., - That is, he was immediately endowed with extraordinary gifts of God's Spirit, as strength, and courage, and wisdom, and other excellent qualities which fitted him for, and put him upon noble attempts.

glossa.text: *Look not.* The elder sons of Isai being rejected, the least is chosen to the kingdom, because, the Jewish priesthood and the kingdom of the former people being despised, Christ was made the head of the lesser people, king and priest.

*The little one.* From the office of the flocks David was made king of men: but Christ was carried over from the sheepfold of the Jewish people to the kingdom of the nations. ((GREG., lib. I Moral., cap. 6; lib. XVIII, cap. 6.)) The devil, although he ever seeks the affliction of the just, etc., *as far as* there is no power but from God.

notes.text: God of Jacob — God had made a covenant with Jacob and his posterity.
Sanctuary — From the tabernacle in Zion, where the ark then was; toward which the Israelites directed their prayers.
Rejoice — Hereby they shew their confidence in God, and their assurance of the victory. Name - To the honour of God. Set up - In way of triumph.

Now — We are already sure of victory by the consideration of God's power and faithfulness and love to David, and to his people. They speak as one person, because they were unanimous in this prayer. Saveth - Will certainly save. Strength - This shews how God will hear him, even by saving him with a strong hand.
Remember — Trust in it.
Brought down — From their horses and chariots, to which they trusted. Stand - Stand firmly, and keep the field.

Let the king — God, the supreme monarch, the king of kings, and in a peculiar manner the king of Israel. A thanksgiving for blessings received, ver. 1-6. An expression of confidence in God, ver. 7-13. To the chief musician, A psalm of David. Title of the psalm. Of David - The subject of this psalm is the same with the former, both being made for the peoples use, concerning the king. Only the prayers there used, are here turned into praises, for the blessings received in answer to their prayers. And as David was an illustrious type of Christ, so in many of these expressions he looks beyond himself to Christ, in whom they are properly, and fully accomplished.

glossa.text: *May he hear thee:* the things which he wills to be done for her in the time of tribulation. *In the day of tribulation,* wherein we pray to God with the greater desire. *Of the God of Jacob,* that as to him, so to thee he may give the grace of blessing, and set thee before the Jews.
*May he send:* the Father. *Help,* by sending the Son.

*Mindful.* He treats as it were of a priest about to offer sacrifice and of a king about to fight. *Of thy sacrifice. ((Ibid.))* He foresaw the sacrifice of the Church, not of cattle, but of the blood and the body of Christ.

*May he give.* Diapsalma, the things which he wishes and affirms for the time of glory. *All thy counsel.* ((AUG.)) Not only in that thou hast laid down thy soul for the life of very many; but also in that *blindness in part hath happened in Israel, and so all Israel should be saved.*
*We shall rejoice. ((Ibid.))* Therefore this prayer, because we shall rejoice and shall be magnified; he shews himself to be one of the Church so long a time before.

*In powers.* ((AUG.)) Our powers are the salvation of his favour, since he gives help even out of tribulation, because vain is the salvation of men, which is of the left hand, whence also pride is born. *The salvation of his right hand.* ((Ibid.)), that is, spiritual grace, etc., *as far as* they who presume upon earthly dignity.

notes.text: Therefore we behave undauntedly — But most of all when we have death in view; knowing that our greatest happiness lies beyond the grave.

For we cannot clearly see him in this life, wherein we walk by faith only: an evidence, indeed, that necessarily implies a kind of "seeing him who is invisible;" yet as far beneath what we shall have in eternity, as it is above that of bare, unassisted reason.
Present with the Lord — This demonstrates that the happiness of the saints is not deferred till the resurrection.
Therefore we are ambitious — The only ambition which has place in a Christian. Whether present - In the body. Or absent - From it.

For we all — Apostles as well as other men, whether now present in the body, or absent from it. Must appear - Openly, without covering, where all hidden things will be revealed; probably the sins, even of the faithful, which were forgiven long before. For many of their good works, as their repentance, their revenge against sin, cannot other wise appear. But this will be done at their own desire, without grief, and without shame. According to what he hath done in the body, whether good or evil - In the body he did either good or evil; in the body he is recompensed accordingly.

glossa.text: *Being confident.* God makes us to will immortality, and makes us also certain through the Spirit, and therefore we are confident. *We are absent from the Lord.* How? when it is written elsewhere: *In him we live, and move, and are? ((Act. XVII.))* Because, although God is everywhere, yet he is not seen here as in heaven. We are absent therefore not by faith, but by sight.

*That every one may render.* Even children, who, if not by themselves, have done by others, while through them they believed or believed not, according to which they are judged, not according to what they were about to do if they lived long. For he says: *according as he hath done in the body,* not as he was about to do if he lived, in vain therefore does a man promise himself after this body what here in the body he neglected to procure. *We persuade.* The apostles persuade that the rest, living well, believe and provide for themselves, because by the perverse speech of certain men the day of the Lord is come into doubt

notes.text: So is the kingdom of God — The inward kingdom is like seed which a man casts into the ground - This a preacher of the Gospel casts into the heart. And he sleeps and rises night and day - That is, he has it continually in his thoughts. Meantime it springs and grows up he knows not how - Even he that sowed it cannot explain how it grows. For as the earth by a curious kind of mechanism, which the greatest philosophers cannot comprehend, does as it were spontaneously bring forth first the blade, then the ear, then the full corn in the ear: so the soul, in an inexplicable manner, brings forth, first weak graces, then stronger, then full holiness: and all this of itself, as a machine, whose spring of motion is within itself. Yet observe the amazing exactness of the comparison. The earth brings forth no corn (as the soul no holiness) without both the care and toil of man, and the benign influence of heaven.
He putteth in the sickle — God cutteth down and gathereth the corn into his garner.
Matt. xiii, 31; Luke xiii, 18.

He spake the word as they were able to hear it — Adapting it to the capacity of his hearers; and speaking as plain as he could without offending them. A rule never to be forgotten by those who instruct others.

glossa.text: *So is the kingdom of God. ((HIER.))* Divine Scripture shows the heavenly sacraments through earthly likenesses, as is plain throughout the whole body of the Gospels. *The kingdom of God* is the Church, which, etc., *as far as: Since the harvest is at hand,* that is, the consummation of the age, in which the just shall rejoice, they that have sown in tears.

*He putteth in the sickle. ((VICT. ANT.))* The harvest indeed is the time of the consummation, the sickle, the word of God, more piercing than any two-edged sword. But the sickle in this place does not denote, etc., *as far as* for all bear wheat, though not all equally much.

*As a grain. ((HIER.))* This seed he compares again to a grain of mustard, which is least in fear, great in charity, which is greater than all herbs, because God is charity, and all flesh is grass, and let him that is weak eat herbs. And it makes the branches of mercy and of compassion. Under whose shadow the poor of Christ, who are the living creatures of heaven, delight to dwell.

*It shall have been sown.* By Christ or by man in the earth, or in the field, that is, in his own heart. This man is our sense and our mind, which, cherishing the grain of preaching with the moisture of faith, makes it sprout in the field of its own breast. *It is less,* etc. As one preaching things contemptible, and at the first he is not believed, because he preaches God a man, dead, crucified, this, compared with the eloquence and the wisdom of the philosophers, is found less.

*It groweth up,* etc. Which in height, in breadth, in length of years surpasses the nature of herbs: it is high, because it lifts up to heavenly things; broad, because it has taken possession of the whole world; full of years, because it shall not be able to be ended. *Than herbs. ((BEDA.))* The philosophic disciplines, which grow up so much the more openly, become the more worthless: because, like the pot-herbs of the grasses, they will quickly fall.

*Without a parable. ((ID.))* Not that he made no discourse plain to the crowds, but because no discourse of his is found in which something of parable is not found.

*But apart, the disciples. ((HIER.))* For they were worthy to hear the mysteries in the innermost sanctuary of wisdom, who, the tumults of their thoughts being removed, abode in the solitude of the virtues. For wisdom is to be learned in a time of leisure.

echoes.text: For God will bring every work into judgment, with every hidden thing, whether it is good, or whether it is evil.
echoes.note: Qoheleth's conclusion that 'God will bring every deed into judgment, with every secret thing, whether good or evil' is closely paralleled by 'each one may receive the things in the body... whether good or bad.' The good/evil pairing and universal accounting are strongly coherent; high volume of shared content makes the judgment-of-deeds echo secure.

echoes.text: Behold, his soul is puffed up. It is not upright in him, but the righteous will live by his faith.
echoes.note: 'We walk by faith, not by sight' restates the Habakkuk principle that the righteous live by faith/faithfulness, a text Paul cites programmatically elsewhere (Rom 1:17; Gal 3:11). The verbal echo is loose but the theological content—life ordered by trust rather than visible evidence—coheres tightly with Habakkuk's contrast between the proud who rely on sight and the faithful who wait.

echoes.text: Also to you, Lord, belongs loving kindness, for you reward every man according to his work.
echoes.note: 'You repay everyone according to what they have done' supplies the recompense logic of the judgment seat where each receives according to deeds. Recurrence is notable: this 'render according to works' formula recurs across the OT (Prov 24:12; Jer 17:10) and Paul invokes it at Rom 2:6, supporting its presence here.

echoes.text: If you say, “Behold, we didn’t know this”; doesn’t he who weighs the hearts consider it? He who keeps your soul, doesn’t he know it? Shall he not render to every man according to his work?
echoes.note: 'Will he not repay everyone according to their deeds?'—God who weighs the heart renders to each by works, matching the judgment-seat recompense. The proverb's emphasis that God sees and requites secret action coheres with Paul's 'revealed before the judgment seat.' Part of a recurrent OT recompense cluster behind 5:10.

echoes.text: I, Yahweh, search the mind, I try the heart, even to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his doings.
echoes.note: 'I the LORD search the heart... to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his deeds.' The heart-searching judge who recompenses deeds undergirds Paul's appearance before Christ's judgment seat. Coherent with the recompense motif and reinforced by recurrence across the OT requital tradition.

echoes.text: With him, I will speak mouth to mouth, even plainly, and not in riddles; and he shall see Yahweh’s form. Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant, against Moses?”
echoes.note: God speaks with Moses 'mouth to mouth, clearly, and not in dark speech,' and Moses 'beholds the form of the LORD'—the privileged sight Paul defers until the believer is 'at home with the Lord.' The faith-now / sight-later structure faintly recalls the Moses-vs-ordinary-prophet distinction. Low volume; contested as a general topos of seeing God rather than a targeted allusion.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Put in the sickle; for the harvest is ripe. Come, tread, for the wine press is full, the vats overflow, for their wickedness is great.”
echoes.note: The harvest climax 'he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come' (4:29) closely echoes Joel's 'Put in the sickle; for the harvest is ripe.' The verbal overlap of sickle-and-ripe-harvest is distinctive (high volume) and coheres with Mark's eschatological framing of the kingdom's arrival as a reaping, making this the pericope's strongest link.

echoes.text: God said, “Let the earth yield grass, herbs yielding seeds, and fruit trees bearing fruit after their kind, with their seeds in it, on the earth”; and it was so. The earth yielded grass, herbs yielding seed after their kind, and trees bearing fruit, with their seeds in it, after their kind; and God saw that it was good.
echoes.note: The earth bearing fruit 'of itself' (automate)—blade, ear, full grain (4:28)—recalls the creation account of the earth bringing forth vegetation yielding seed after its kind. The motif of the earth's God-given autonomous fertility is thematically coherent, though Mark gives no verbal citation.

echoes.text: “‘When you reap the harvest of your land, you shall not wholly reap the corners of your field, neither shall you gather the gleanings of your harvest.
echoes.note: The image of grain ripening to harvest draws on the broader Torah harvest framework, but the link is generic. Included for maximality; volume and distinctiveness are low and the coherence is only with the agricultural setting.

echoes.text: in the mountain of the height of Israel will I plant it; and it shall produce boughs, and bear fruit, and be a goodly cedar: and under it shall dwell all birds of every wing; in the shade of its branches shall they dwell.
echoes.note: The mustard plant that puts out 'great branches, so that the birds of the sky can lodge under its shadow' (4:32) reworks Ezekiel's noble cedar planted on the mountain under which 'all birds of every wing' dwell in the shadow of its branches. The branches-shadow-birds-nesting cluster is verbally and thematically tight (high volume), and the imperial-tree-as-kingdom motif coheres with Mark's kingdom parable.

echoes.text: The leaves of it were beautiful, and its fruit much, and in it was food for all: the animals of the field had shadow under it, and the birds of the sky lived in its branches, and all flesh was fed from it.
echoes.note: Nebuchadnezzar's tree whose branches shelter the beasts and in which 'the birds of the sky lived' supplies the proverbial great-tree-with-nesting-birds image behind 4:32. The recurrence of this kingdom-tree topos (Daniel 4:21 repeats it) gives strong availability and coherence with the contrast between the tiny seed and the sheltering kingdom.

echoes.text: All the birds of the sky made their nests in its boughs; and under its branches all the animals of the field gave birth to their young; and all great nations lived under its shadow.
echoes.note: Ezekiel's Assyrian cedar in whose boughs 'all the birds of the sky made their nests' and under whose shadow great nations lived belongs to the same world-tree tradition Mark evokes. The shared birds-nest-in-the-shadow image reinforces recurrence across the prophetic kingdom-tree corpus.

echoes.text: whose leaves were beautiful, and its fruit much, and in it was food for all; under which the animals of the field lived, and on whose branches the birds of the sky had their habitation:
echoes.note: The reprise of the tree 'in whose branches the birds of the sky lived' restates the Danielic kingdom-tree, strengthening the topos behind 4:32 by recurrence within a single source. Its function is to confirm the availability of the great-tree-as-dominion symbol rather than to add new wording.

echoes.text: The birds of the sky nest by them. They sing among the branches.
echoes.note: The psalm's 'birds of the sky' that nest by the branches and sing reflects the same creation-poetic image of birds lodging in foliage. It is a faint, generic parallel that adds coherence to the nesting-birds detail but lacks the kingdom-tree distinctiveness of Ezekiel and Daniel.

echoes.text: I will open my mouth in a parable. I will utter dark sayings of old,
echoes.note: The summary that Jesus spoke 'without a parable he didn't speak to them' resonates with the psalmist's 'I will open my mouth in a parable; I will utter dark sayings of old.' The link between exclusive parabolic teaching and revealed/concealed wisdom is thematically coherent, though for Mark it is faint and uncited.

notes.text: The highest branch — Of the royal seed; of the highest branch that is heir to the throne; namely, the Messiah. An high mountain - Upon Mount Zion. Eminent - Not for outward splendour, but for spiritual advantages.
In the mountain — In Jerusalem. All fowl - All nations. In the shadow - There they shall find peace and safety.

The trees — The great ones on earth. The high tree - The kingdom of Babylon, which was brought low indeed, when overthrown by Darius and Cyrus. God reproves a corrupt proverb, ver. 1-4. It shall be well with the righteous, ver. 5-9. but ill with the wicked man, tho' he had a good father, ver. 10-13. It shall be well with a good man, tho' he had a wicked father, ver. 14-18. Therefore God is righteous, ver. 19-20. It shall be well with penitents, but ill with apostates, ver. 21-29. An exhortation to repentance, ver. 30-32.

glossa.text: *It is good to confess.* ((CASS.)) First, he treats how the good man, being untroubled, keeps the sabbath of the mind, perceiving that all things are done well by God, which the foolish man does not know. ((AUG.)) The good things of the present, given to us by God, are a consolation: when they are lacking, it is justice. For God both consoles us, and amends us: in both, therefore, let us be thankful to him, saying: *It is good to confess,* etc.

*Upon the ten-stringed instrument.* ((ID.)) He sings a psalm who does good with cheerfulness. He with whom it is done in sadness does not himself do it: and he carries the psaltery, he does not sing upon it. *Upon the ten-stringed instrument.* If thou only speakest well, it is a canticle without the harp; if thou workest, and speakest not, it is a harp without the canticle; and therefore both speak well and do well.

*For thou hast delighted.* ((ID.)) Whence the Apostle: *We are his own moulding,* etc., *as far as: How great are thy works. In thy handiwork.* ((CASS., HIER.)) Both in the beauty of the fabric of the world itself, and in its obedience, and in its ordering, and in its causes, and in its effects, and in the works of the hands which I use *uior*, or which I marvel at.

notes.text: Therefore we behave undauntedly — But most of all when we have death in view; knowing that our greatest happiness lies beyond the grave.

For we cannot clearly see him in this life, wherein we walk by faith only: an evidence, indeed, that necessarily implies a kind of "seeing him who is invisible;" yet as far beneath what we shall have in eternity, as it is above that of bare, unassisted reason.
Present with the Lord — This demonstrates that the happiness of the saints is not deferred till the resurrection.
Therefore we are ambitious — The only ambition which has place in a Christian. Whether present - In the body. Or absent - From it.

For we all — Apostles as well as other men, whether now present in the body, or absent from it. Must appear - Openly, without covering, where all hidden things will be revealed; probably the sins, even of the faithful, which were forgiven long before. For many of their good works, as their repentance, their revenge against sin, cannot other wise appear. But this will be done at their own desire, without grief, and without shame. According to what he hath done in the body, whether good or evil - In the body he did either good or evil; in the body he is recompensed accordingly.

glossa.text: *Being confident.* God makes us to will immortality, and makes us also certain through the Spirit, and therefore we are confident. *We are absent from the Lord.* How? when it is written elsewhere: *In him we live, and move, and are? ((Act. XVII.))* Because, although God is everywhere, yet he is not seen here as in heaven. We are absent therefore not by faith, but by sight.

*That every one may render.* Even children, who, if not by themselves, have done by others, while through them they believed or believed not, according to which they are judged, not according to what they were about to do if they lived long. For he says: *according as he hath done in the body,* not as he was about to do if he lived, in vain therefore does a man promise himself after this body what here in the body he neglected to procure. *We persuade.* The apostles persuade that the rest, living well, believe and provide for themselves, because by the perverse speech of certain men the day of the Lord is come into doubt

notes.text: So is the kingdom of God — The inward kingdom is like seed which a man casts into the ground - This a preacher of the Gospel casts into the heart. And he sleeps and rises night and day - That is, he has it continually in his thoughts. Meantime it springs and grows up he knows not how - Even he that sowed it cannot explain how it grows. For as the earth by a curious kind of mechanism, which the greatest philosophers cannot comprehend, does as it were spontaneously bring forth first the blade, then the ear, then the full corn in the ear: so the soul, in an inexplicable manner, brings forth, first weak graces, then stronger, then full holiness: and all this of itself, as a machine, whose spring of motion is within itself. Yet observe the amazing exactness of the comparison. The earth brings forth no corn (as the soul no holiness) without both the care and toil of man, and the benign influence of heaven.
He putteth in the sickle — God cutteth down and gathereth the corn into his garner.
Matt. xiii, 31; Luke xiii, 18.

He spake the word as they were able to hear it — Adapting it to the capacity of his hearers; and speaking as plain as he could without offending them. A rule never to be forgotten by those who instruct others.

glossa.text: *So is the kingdom of God. ((HIER.))* Divine Scripture shows the heavenly sacraments through earthly likenesses, as is plain throughout the whole body of the Gospels. *The kingdom of God* is the Church, which, etc., *as far as: Since the harvest is at hand,* that is, the consummation of the age, in which the just shall rejoice, they that have sown in tears.

*He putteth in the sickle. ((VICT. ANT.))* The harvest indeed is the time of the consummation, the sickle, the word of God, more piercing than any two-edged sword. But the sickle in this place does not denote, etc., *as far as* for all bear wheat, though not all equally much.

*As a grain. ((HIER.))* This seed he compares again to a grain of mustard, which is least in fear, great in charity, which is greater than all herbs, because God is charity, and all flesh is grass, and let him that is weak eat herbs. And it makes the branches of mercy and of compassion. Under whose shadow the poor of Christ, who are the living creatures of heaven, delight to dwell.

*It shall have been sown.* By Christ or by man in the earth, or in the field, that is, in his own heart. This man is our sense and our mind, which, cherishing the grain of preaching with the moisture of faith, makes it sprout in the field of its own breast. *It is less,* etc. As one preaching things contemptible, and at the first he is not believed, because he preaches God a man, dead, crucified, this, compared with the eloquence and the wisdom of the philosophers, is found less.

*It groweth up,* etc. Which in height, in breadth, in length of years surpasses the nature of herbs: it is high, because it lifts up to heavenly things; broad, because it has taken possession of the whole world; full of years, because it shall not be able to be ended. *Than herbs. ((BEDA.))* The philosophic disciplines, which grow up so much the more openly, become the more worthless: because, like the pot-herbs of the grasses, they will quickly fall.

*Without a parable. ((ID.))* Not that he made no discourse plain to the crowds, but because no discourse of his is found in which something of parable is not found.

*But apart, the disciples. ((HIER.))* For they were worthy to hear the mysteries in the innermost sanctuary of wisdom, who, the tumults of their thoughts being removed, abode in the solitude of the virtues. For wisdom is to be learned in a time of leisure.

echoes.note: 'Will he not repay everyone according to their deeds?'—God who weighs the heart renders to each by works, matching the judgment-seat recompense. The proverb's emphasis that God sees and requites secret action coheres with Paul's 'revealed before the judgment seat.' Part of a recurrent OT recompense cluster behind 5:10.

echoes.text: I, Yahweh, search the mind, I try the heart, even to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his doings.
echoes.note: 'I the LORD search the heart... to give every man according to his ways, according to the fruit of his deeds.' The heart-searching judge who recompenses deeds undergirds Paul's appearance before Christ's judgment seat. Coherent with the recompense motif and reinforced by recurrence across the OT requital tradition.

echoes.text: With him, I will speak mouth to mouth, even plainly, and not in riddles; and he shall see Yahweh’s form. Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant, against Moses?”
echoes.note: God speaks with Moses 'mouth to mouth, clearly, and not in dark speech,' and Moses 'beholds the form of the LORD'—the privileged sight Paul defers until the believer is 'at home with the Lord.' The faith-now / sight-later structure faintly recalls the Moses-vs-ordinary-prophet distinction. Low volume; contested as a general topos of seeing God rather than a targeted allusion.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Put in the sickle; for the harvest is ripe. Come, tread, for the wine press is full, the vats overflow, for their wickedness is great.”
echoes.note: The harvest climax 'he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come' (4:29) closely echoes Joel's 'Put in the sickle; for the harvest is ripe.' The verbal overlap of sickle-and-ripe-harvest is distinctive (high volume) and coheres with Mark's eschatological framing of the kingdom's arrival as a reaping, making this the pericope's strongest link.

echoes.text: God said, “Let the earth yield grass, herbs yielding seeds, and fruit trees bearing fruit after their kind, with their seeds in it, on the earth”; and it was so. The earth yielded grass, herbs yielding seed after their kind, and trees bearing fruit, with their seeds in it, after their kind; and God saw that it was good.
echoes.note: The earth bearing fruit 'of itself' (automate)—blade, ear, full grain (4:28)—recalls the creation account of the earth bringing forth vegetation yielding seed after its kind. The motif of the earth's God-given autonomous fertility is thematically coherent, though Mark gives no verbal citation.

echoes.text: “‘When you reap the harvest of your land, you shall not wholly reap the corners of your field, neither shall you gather the gleanings of your harvest.
echoes.note: The image of grain ripening to harvest draws on the broader Torah harvest framework, but the link is generic. Included for maximality; volume and distinctiveness are low and the coherence is only with the agricultural setting.

echoes.text: in the mountain of the height of Israel will I plant it; and it shall produce boughs, and bear fruit, and be a goodly cedar: and under it shall dwell all birds of every wing; in the shade of its branches shall they dwell.
echoes.note: The mustard plant that puts out 'great branches, so that the birds of the sky can lodge under its shadow' (4:32) reworks Ezekiel's noble cedar planted on the mountain under which 'all birds of every wing' dwell in the shadow of its branches. The branches-shadow-birds-nesting cluster is verbally and thematically tight (high volume), and the imperial-tree-as-kingdom motif coheres with Mark's kingdom parable.

echoes.text: The leaves of it were beautiful, and its fruit much, and in it was food for all: the animals of the field had shadow under it, and the birds of the sky lived in its branches, and all flesh was fed from it.
echoes.note: Nebuchadnezzar's tree whose branches shelter the beasts and in which 'the birds of the sky lived' supplies the proverbial great-tree-with-nesting-birds image behind 4:32. The recurrence of this kingdom-tree topos (Daniel 4:21 repeats it) gives strong availability and coherence with the contrast between the tiny seed and the sheltering kingdom.

echoes.text: All the birds of the sky made their nests in its boughs; and under its branches all the animals of the field gave birth to their young; and all great nations lived under its shadow.
echoes.note: Ezekiel's Assyrian cedar in whose boughs 'all the birds of the sky made their nests' and under whose shadow great nations lived belongs to the same world-tree tradition Mark evokes. The shared birds-nest-in-the-shadow image reinforces recurrence across the prophetic kingdom-tree corpus.

echoes.text: whose leaves were beautiful, and its fruit much, and in it was food for all; under which the animals of the field lived, and on whose branches the birds of the sky had their habitation:
echoes.note: The reprise of the tree 'in whose branches the birds of the sky lived' restates the Danielic kingdom-tree, strengthening the topos behind 4:32 by recurrence within a single source. Its function is to confirm the availability of the great-tree-as-dominion symbol rather than to add new wording.

echoes.text: The birds of the sky nest by them. They sing among the branches.
echoes.note: The psalm's 'birds of the sky' that nest by the branches and sing reflects the same creation-poetic image of birds lodging in foliage. It is a faint, generic parallel that adds coherence to the nesting-birds detail but lacks the kingdom-tree distinctiveness of Ezekiel and Daniel.

echoes.text: I will open my mouth in a parable. I will utter dark sayings of old,
echoes.note: The summary that Jesus spoke 'without a parable he didn't speak to them' resonates with the psalmist's 'I will open my mouth in a parable; I will utter dark sayings of old.' The link between exclusive parabolic teaching and revealed/concealed wisdom is thematically coherent, though for Mark it is faint and uncited.

registers.label: Spare
lines: Some trust in chariots, and some in horses.
But our trust is in the name of the Lord our God.
God does not see as we see; we look at the face.
The Lord looks on the heart.
A scattered seed grows while the sower sleeps.
The kingdom of God is coming, small and sure.
Come, let us worship the God of hidden growth.
We come to be planted and to grow. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: A farmer scatters seed and goes to bed, and night after night, without his knowing how, the green stalk pushes up through the dark soil.
The kingdom of God is like a seed.
You cannot tell by looking who God is calling; Samuel passed over the tall sons, and God chose the youngest, out in the field with the sheep.
The kingdom of God is like a seed.
The smallest seed of all becomes a shrub so wide the birds of the air come and nest in its shade.
The kingdom of God is like a seed.
So bring what little you have, a mustard grain of faith, and let God do the growing.
The kingdom of God is like a seed, and we have come to be planted.

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: We trust no chariots; we trust the name of the Lord.
Small and sure, the kingdom grows.
God passes by the tall and chooses the heart.
Small and sure, the kingdom grows.
The seed sprouts while the sower sleeps.
Small and sure, the kingdom grows.
Come, let us worship the God who plants us.
Small and sure, the kingdom grows. Amen.
